records.value:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) relate the structure of gaseous exchange sites in plants to their function,
b) describe the mechanism of opening and closing of stomata in plants,
c) investigate aerobic and anaerobic respiration in living organisms,
d) explain the economic importance of anaerobic respiration in nature,
e) appreciate the significance of gaseous exchange and respiration to plants and the environment.

records.why: Checked: a submerged leaf holds mostly air in its air spaces; bubbles were never collected or tested in any lesson, so naming them as CO2 or O2 overstated the evidence. records.old: (a) Respiration and photosynthesis are controlled by enzymes. In warm water the enzyme molecules and their substrate molecules have more kinetic energy and collide more often, so more reactions succeed each second. More gas is produced and more bubbles appear. In cold water the enzymes work slowly, so little gas is made and few bubbles appear. (b) Carbon dioxide is made by cellular respiration in the mitochondria of mesophyll cells. Oxygen is made by photosynthesis in the chloroplasts, but this needs light, so it only happens if the submerged leaf is lit. Some CO2 from respiration would also dissolve in the water, so fewer CO2 bubbles would be seen than the amount actually made. We did not test the bubbles from the leaf (for example with limewater), so we cannot be certain of their contents. Our best explanation, based on the yeast evidence and what we know about leaf cells, is that the bubbles are mostly gas released from leaf cells and air spaces through the stomata, with CO2 from respiration and, in light, O2 from photosynthesis possibly contributing. (c) The Lesson 6 investigation tested temperature: yeast in warm sugar-cane juice produced significantly more CO2 bubbles per minute than yeast in cold water, so respiration rate increased with warmth, matching the sukuma wiki pattern. The Lesson 4 limewater test compared aerobic and anaerobic conditions, not temperature, so it shows that respiration makes CO2 but does not itself show the temperature effect (though warming also made the limewater turn milky faster). The balloon bottles with different yeast concentrations also inflated because of CO2 from yeast, showing that more yeast gave faster gas production, but they did not vary temperature. So the Lesson 6 data support the idea that temperature controls respiration rate through enzyme activity.
records.new: (a) Respiration and photosynthesis are controlled by enzymes. In cold water the enzymes work slowly, so less gas is made. Warmth also makes the air inside the leaf expand and makes gases less soluble in water, so more gas can leave the leaf as bubbles. Our tests did not separate these effects. (b) Carbon dioxide is made by cellular respiration in the mitochondria of mesophyll cells, and it needs glucose and oxygen. Oxygen is made by photosynthesis in the chloroplasts, and it needs light, carbon dioxide and water, so it only happens if the submerged leaf is lit. Gas from the air spaces inside the leaf could also leave through the stomata. We did not test the bubbles from the leaf (for example with limewater), so we cannot be certain of their contents. Our best explanation, based on the yeast evidence and what we know about leaf cells, is that the bubbles are mostly gas released from the leaf's air spaces through the stomata, with CO2 from respiration and, in light, O2 from photosynthesis possibly contributing. (c) The Lesson 6 investigation tested temperature: yeast in warm sugar-cane juice produced significantly more CO2 bubbles per minute than yeast in cold water, so respiration rate increased with warmth, matching the sukuma wiki pattern. The Lesson 4 limewater test compared aerobic and anaerobic conditions with both tubes at the same temperature, so it shows that respiration makes CO2, even without oxygen, but it does not show a temperature effect. records.new: Learners handling hot water must use heat-resistant gloves or cloths and place beakers on stable surfaces away from the edge of the bench. records.why: The practical content that replaces the old five options. Materials are the ones already used in Lessons 4 to 6 and 9 (yeast, sugar, balloons, bottles, tubing, pH strips, uji), so they are available in partner schools. Biogas gas collects slowly, so the plan uses a head-start bottle and later readings rather than promising a result in 35 minutes.
records.old: Possible investigation types include: (A) Effect of temperature on bubble rate — sukuma wiki leaf discs submerged in water at 10°C, 25°C, and 40°C; bubbles counted per minute at each temperature using a stopwatch; (B) Stomatal distribution — nail varnish peel method on upper and lower surfaces of sukuma wiki, bean, or maize leaves; stomata counted under a hand lens or microscope in a defined field of view; (C) Effect of blocking stomata — petroleum jelly applied to upper surface only, lower surface only, both surfaces, or neither; leaf discs submerged; bubble rate compared; (D) Detection of CO₂ in respiration — germinating beans (githeri seeds soaked overnight) placed in a sealed flask; hydrogencarbonate indicator or lime water used to detect CO₂ after 15 minutes; (E) Heat production in respiration — temperature probe or thermometer placed in a flask of germinating githeri seeds vs. boiled (dead) seeds.
records.new: Groups work on the track they chose in Lesson 9. (A) Yeast fermentation: 5 g sugar and 1 g yeast in 100 mL warm water in a bottle with a balloon or a delivery tube into water; each group changes one variable (water temperature of about 10, 25 to 30 and 40°C from baths the teacher prepared; or sugar amount; or yeast amount; or a 1 cm cooking-oil layer to exclude air) and records bubbles per minute or balloon circumference every 5 minutes. (B) Biogas simulation: a bottle of chopped kitchen scraps or cow dung slurry in water, with a delivery tube to an inverted water-filled bottle; because gas collects slowly, groups record the start level, temperature and smell now, compare with a teacher-prepared bottle started 2 to 3 days earlier, and take further readings on the following days. (C) Food fermentation: cooled uji (millet or maize flour porridge) kept in a warm place and a cool place; pH strip, smell and appearance are recorded at the start and every 15 minutes and compared with the teacher-prepared 24-hour jars from Lesson 9; no tasting.
